articles.title: Why You Keep Waiting for the Right Moment to Speak Up
articles.excerpt: You are in a meeting and you have a good point. You can feel it sitting right there. You just need the right moment to jump in. So you wait for a pause. Then someone else takes the pause. You wait for…
articles.body: You are in a meeting and you have a good point. You can feel it sitting right there. You just need the right moment to jump in. So you wait for a pause. Then someone else takes the pause. You wait for the topic to come back around. It moves on. Ten minutes later a coworker says almost exactly what you were thinking, and everyone nods. You leave the meeting annoyed at yourself, and a little more convinced that you are just not a speak up kind of person. You are not missing some talent other people have. You are waiting for a signal that your brain was trained never to give you. Your brain is waiting for proof it is safe. It will never find enough. There is a part of your brain called the reticular activating system, the RAS.

articles.title: Terraform state is the real production database
articles.excerpt: A friend describes Terraform state as the database nobody backs up. I think about that every time I see a local state file in a repo. The baseline I now refuse to work without: Remote state with locki…
articles.body: A friend describes Terraform state as the database nobody backs up. I think about that every time I see a local state file in a repo. The baseline I now refuse to work without: Remote state with locking. S3 + DynamoDB is boring and correct. One state per environment , never a shared state with workspaces pretending. An import path that doesn't require editing state by hand. Drift detection on a schedule , not when someone notices. The failure I've seen twice: someone imports a resource into the wrong state, and the next apply tries to recreate production. Locking doesn't help if the lock is on the wrong file. The other thing: state contains secrets in plaintext. If the bucket isn't encrypted and access-controlled, you have a leak. It's not glamorous, but the state is the system.
articles.author: Frida Hansen

articles.title: ISO 13485 or ISO 9001? The Capabilities That Decide the Answer
articles.excerpt: Two factories send you certificates. One holds ISO 13485:2016, the other ISO 9001:2026. Both are current. When a design change lands on the line, one can show what was re-verified and the other cannot…
articles.body: Two factories send you certificates. One holds ISO 13485:2016, the other ISO 9001:2026. Both are current. When a design change lands on the line, one can show what was re-verified and the other cannot — and the certificate will not say which. That gap is the real ISO 13485 vs ISO 9001 question for a medical device QMS supplier. Which capabilities actually separate the two systems? • Design control. ISO 13485 requires it, covering design inputs, outputs, verification, validation, transfer and change control. ISO 9001 allows design to be excluded from scope entirely — and with design excluded, there is no design baseline, so the concept of a "change" has nothing to attach to. • Risk management.

articles.body: In September 2026, I released rspec-wasm , a tool for running RSpec tests on ruby.wasm, and introduced it in my previous DEV article: Stop Writing Ruby Tests in JS Template Literals: Meet rspec-wasm I've now released rspec-wasm v0.2.0 , which adds support for asynchronous JavaScript setup and teardown around RSpec execution. One of the great advantages of building applications with WebAssembly is the ability to combine functionality from different Wasm modules. However, until now, rspec-wasm had no way to asynchronously initialize an external runtime before running RSpec tests or clean it up afterward. With v0.2.0, we can initialize external JavaScript or Wasm runtimes before running RSpec, making it possible to test Ruby code that interacts with them.

articles.title: A checklist before you ship a notebook model
articles.excerpt: I've shipped enough models from notebooks to know that the notebook is the least of it. Six checks I run before anything goes to a service: Snapshot the data. The exact table or file, with a hash. "It…
articles.body: I've shipped enough models from notebooks to know that the notebook is the least of it. Six checks I run before anything goes to a service: Snapshot the data. The exact table or file, with a hash. "It was in BigQuery" is not reproducible. Freeze an eval set. Not the test split from training — a small, ugly, real-world one. Check the input distribution. Compare the serving inputs to the training inputs; the drift is usually in the tail. Measure the serving path, not the model. p50 and p99 end to end. Write down the failure behavior. What returns when the model is uncertain, slow, or wrong? Plan the rollback. A model that can't be turned off in minutes is a liability. None of this is novel. It's just the list I forget when I'm excited about the notebook. What's on your pre-ship list?

articles.title: How to deploy a FastAPI app on Ownkube
articles.excerpt: FastAPI is fast to run locally with uvicorn app.main:app --reload, and the production version of that command is not much longer. Production adds three things: a process manager that restarts a crashe…
articles.body: FastAPI is fast to run locally with uvicorn app.main:app --reload , and the production version of that command is not much longer. Production adds three things: a process manager that restarts a crashed worker, config read from environment variables instead of a .env file in the repo, and a health check for the platform to poll. Ownkube handles the rest from a git push. This walks through deploying a FastAPI app on Ownkube Compute: running Gunicorn with Uvicorn workers, configuring settings through environment variables , adding a health check endpoint, and turning on autoscaling . TL;DR Push a FastAPI app with a Dockerfile , and Ownkube builds it, deploys it, and issues TLS automatically on your *.ownkube.app hostname.

articles.title: Planetary defense: How military and civil satellites are watching fireballs to help keep Earth safe from space rocks
articles.excerpt: Satellites are watching fireballs blaze through Earth's atmosphere, strengthening planetary defense knowhow and helping scientists learn more about space debris impacts.
articles.body: It came from outer space, exploding high above the South Atlantic off the coast of Argentina. That April 1 event — an incoming meteor , also termed a bolide — was observed by both U.S. space-based military and civil sensors. Hush-hush U.S. government satellite sensors detected the speedy fireball cutting through our atmosphere. The object's brightness peaked at an altitude of nearly 60 miles (90.5 kilometers) over the South Atlantic. That dazzling spectacle was also caught by the National Atmospheric and Oceanic Administration's GOES-E and Europe's Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) Imager-1 satellite. Those two independent spacecraft in geostationary orbit detected the bolide via onboard lightning imagers.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 1, 1962: The Soviet Union Launches Mars 1 spacecraft to Red Planet during the Space Race
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet. While it did end up flying by Mars , the mission was not exactly a success. After it separated from the rocket, it deployed its solar panels and started cruising toward Mars. When mission controllers were checking out the telemetry it transmitted back to Earth, they found out that Mars 1 had sprung a leak in one of the gas valves that controls the spacecraft's orientation. And without a working orientation system, Mars 1 would have a hard time pointing its antennas in the right direction. It lost contact with Earth when it was about halfway to Mars . A model of Mars 1, a Mars flyby spacecraft launched to the Red Planet by the Soviet Union on Nov. 1, 1962.

articles.title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
articles.excerpt: It's still unknown how attackers got access to Anthropic's verified Cursor account.
articles.body: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident. The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont.
